units: the person the message is addressed to teaches a manual trade to beginners
the beginners lose control of the movement as soon as they are no longer guided
the writer blames the way the trade is taught rather than the learners
the demonstration is currently run straight through, with no pause
the proposed remedy is to break the run of movements into three parts
each part ends with a cue the learner can perceive and check alone
a short scoring sheet, filled in by the learner, separates a good movement from a rough one
the writer advises keeping the split in writing for the next group
text: Dear colleague, I owe you an answer about the beginners who lose the movement the moment you let go of their hands. The fault sits in the method, not in how hard they concentrate. You run the whole sequence through in one go, then ask them to copy it in a single sweep, and the memory of the motion cannot keep up. Break the run into three stretches, and end each one with a cue they can check on their own, the tool resting at a set angle or a sound you only hear when it goes right. They stop, they check, they carry on. Add a short scoring sheet they fill in themselves, one that tells a movement done right from a movement done roughly. Give them a week of fumbling and most will hold the whole run unaided. Keep a written copy of your split, since the next group will need it. Tell me whether it survives your bench and I will mend it.

units: the first question sets one-to-one teaching against teaching a whole group
one-to-one teaching matches the pace to the learner and catches a mistake as it appears
the group setting puts the learner in front of how the others reason
the group setting forces each learner to say out loud what he thought he had mastered
one-to-one teaching costs a great deal because it ties up one instructor per learner
the group setting shares the effort but thins out the instructor's attention
the managers questioned advise alternating the two arrangements
one single marking scheme applied to both arrangements distorts the comparison
text: A listener asks whether teaching one to one beats teaching a whole group. That turns on what you measure. Tutoring matches the pace to the learner and catches a mistake before it hardens into habit, so practical skills come on quickly. A group does something else. It sets each learner in front of the way the others reason, and it forces them to say out loud what they assumed they had mastered. A second question concerns cost. Tutoring ties up one instructor per learner, which keeps it scarce, whereas a group shares the effort and thins the instructor's attention. So must one be picked? The managers questioned advise alternating: the group session lays down the common markers, and the private one clears the blockages a group leaves untouched. A last question turns to assessment. One marking scheme for both arrangements distorts the comparison, since they do not aim at the same gain.

units: an employee at a bookbinding workshop recounts an exchange with a visitor
the visitor wanted to know what the training covers
the employee sorts the learning into three groups
the first group covers knowing the materials and the marks left by old workshops
the second group covers carrying out the movements
the third group comes down to stamina, and that is the one that makes people give up
half the apprentices give up before their first season ends
people leave at the point where the apprentice is asked to decide with nothing to copy
the employee judges success by the absence of fingerprints on the leather
text: An attendant at a bookbinding workshop recounts an exchange with a visitor. She wanted to know what the training covers. He told her it sorts into three groups. The first has to do with the stuff itself: telling one paper from another, picking a glue, reading the marks an old workshop left behind. The second is the hands: folding without crushing, stitching at an even pitch, pressing a cover without bruising it. The third, he said, comes down to stamina, and that is the one that wears people down. She asked how many apprentices give up. Half of them leave before their first season ends, he answered, usually at the point where nobody shows them anything anymore and they have to decide with nothing to copy. She asked what the surest sign of success is. He pointed to the leather: an apprentice sure of his hands leaves no fingerprints on it.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: at the outset the learner lodged with his master to learn a trade
the learner watched for several seasons before being allowed a tool
trade bodies then imposed stages and a fixed length of training
the learner had to submit a finished piece to the judgement of seasoned craftsmen
a refusal forced the learner to start his piece over
as workshops grew, the master could no longer follow each learner
the tricks of the trade were then set down in written manuals
technical schools took over next, with syllabuses and examinations
the shift brought steadiness and cost some of the attention given to one learner
text: To begin with, learning a trade looked nothing like school. You moved in with a master, slept under his roof, and watched him work for whole seasons before anyone let you touch a tool. Then came the trade bodies, which set out stages, tests and a fixed length of training. A learner had to hand in a finished piece for the seasoned men to judge, and if they turned it down, he started over. Workshops grew, and no master had the time to follow each learner, so the tricks of the trade were written down in manuals and the learner had to puzzle them out alone. Technical schools arrived last, with their syllabuses, their classes and their examinations. At every step something steady was gained, and a little of the attention the old master gave his one learner was lost. The argument is far from settled.

units: reading a chapter again wrongly convinces you that you own it
how familiar the text feels gets mistaken for having memorised it
rereading calls on recognition while the test calls for recall
recognition comes so easily that the learner breaks off revising too soon
the learner then finds out what he is missing while sitting the test
saying the content back from memory with the book shut exposes the gaps
the difficulty felt during recall strengthens the memory
the practical consequence is turning each page into a question put to yourself
learners trained this way hold on to more a year later without revising any longer
text: Reading a chapter again gives you the feeling that you own it. The text turns familiar, your eyes slide along, and that ease gets mistaken for real memory. Researchers on learning explain where the muddle starts: rereading calls on recognition, while the test calls for recall. Those are two different operations. Recognition comes easy, so the learner breaks off revising too soon and finds the gap only once the paper sits in front of him. Shut the book, try to say the content back from memory, and the opposite happens. The effort hurts, it exposes the holes, and that very difficulty sets the trace deeper. One practical consequence follows: turn each page you have read into a question you put to yourself. Learners trained that way hold on to more a year later, without having revised any longer than the rest.

units: a pupil was stuck on the same line for the whole lesson
his voice grew fainter as his embarrassment grew
the usual teacher took him for a slow pupil
a teacher passing through looked at the way he held the page
the pupil tilted the sheet and followed the line with his fingernail
the teacher gave him a strip of card with a slot cut into it
the slot laid over the line stopped the words from jostling one another
the pupil first said the letters one by one, then read a whole sentence
the teacher left a description of the method on a card in a drawer
text: The boy had been stuck on the same line since the lesson began. He droned out the syllables, went back, lost his place, and his voice dropped as his embarrassment rose. The schoolmaster saw nothing but a slow pupil. A stand-in teacher, there for a week, watched the way he held the page: he tilted the sheet and traced the line with his fingernail. She handed him a strip of card with a slot cut into it. The boy slid the slot over the line, and the words stopped jostling one another. He said the letters one by one at first, then joined the syllables, then read a whole sentence without stopping for breath. She said nothing about it, but she wrote the method on a card and left it in the drawer of the platform desk. Two seasons on, the boy was reading aloud to his class without a stumble.

units: the reader must settle on one of the two methods and stay with it
the first method rests on writing the list out again and again
once the list is covered, you write it back from memory and then check it
the first method suits runs that are short
the second method means making up cards with a question and an answer
you answer aloud and set aside the cards you have got right
the second method holds off forgetting better on long runs
one identical mock test after a week decides between the two methods
using both together would make it impossible to tell which one worked
text: Before you set out to memorise a list of terms, pick one of two methods and stay with it to the end. First method: copy it out. Write the list in full, cover it, then write down again whatever you can call up. Compare, cross out what went wrong, and start over on a clean sheet. This one puts the hand to work and suits short runs. Second method: question yourself. Cut the list into cards, one item per card, question on one side and answer on the other. Shuffle them, answer aloud, and set aside every card you have got right. This one holds off forgetting better on long runs. Put them side by side after a week, on the same mock test, and keep whichever leaves you hesitating less. Whatever you do, avoid running both in that first week, or you will never know which one did the work.

units: a training centre fitted out in a former market hall received journalists
the woman in charge set out three pieces of work under way
the first covers taking in adults who are switching trades
half of these adults have not studied since they left school
the second reorganised the workshops so that every bench is in view
that clear view makes hazardous handling easier to watch over
the third brings forward the check on what has been learned, judged far too late
a short check now closes every session and gives a marker to measure against
one-to-one support entrusted to former learners is meant to cut the number who drop out
text: Housed in a former market hall, a training centre opened its doors to the press. Its director set out three pieces of work under way. The first concerns intake: the centre now takes in adults switching trades, half of whom have not studied since they left school. The second concerns the premises. The workshops have been laid out so that every bench stays in view from the central aisle, which makes hazardous handling easier to watch over. The third targets assessment, which instructors judged to come far too late; a short check now closes every session and gives the learner a marker to measure himself against. Asked about the people who drop out, the director admitted the numbers stay high through the first season. She announced one-to-one support entrusted to former learners, who know the obstacles because they cleared them themselves.

units: a low room with whitewashed walls serves as a writing workshop for adults
each table is laid out with a sheet, a pencil and a book of models
the leader draws a letter of unusual size on the board
the participants go through the book of models before writing anything at all
each of them then copies the letter ten times over, watching the tilt of the pencil
halfway through the session the leader corrects the position of their wrists
the strokes grow steadier as the session goes on
each of them cuts out his best line and glues it into a shared notebook
the shared notebook hangs near the door of the room
text: A low room with whitewashed walls serves as a writing workshop for a group of adults. Before they arrive, each table holds a blank sheet, a sharpened pencil and a book of models. The leader opens the shutters, then draws a single letter on the board at an unusual size. The participants come in, settle down, and start by leafing through the book of models without writing anything at all. Each of them then copies the letter ten times over, watching the tilt of the pencil. Halfway through the session the leader walks between the rows and straightens their wrists. The sheets fill with strokes, uneven at first, then steadier. At the end, each of them cuts out his best line and glues it into a shared notebook that hangs near the door. The room empties, the pencils go back in their box, and the notebook keeps the record.

units: the writer disputes the idea of replacing general subjects with short courses
these short courses are cut to fit one particular job
what a job consists of changes over the course of a working life
training that fits too snugly turns useless once the equipment changes
the abilities that last are reading a stiff manual and reasoning over a drawing
putting a clean question to a colleague is one of these lasting abilities
these abilities come by a long detour and look pointless while they are taught
looking pointless is what makes them easy to cut from a syllabus
the writer holds that practice with no theoretical detour turns out interchangeable hands
text: Everyone keeps saying that school ought to prepare people for work, and a hasty conclusion gets drawn from it: swap the general subjects for short courses cut to fit one particular job. The intention makes sense, the result is a disaster. A job changes what it consists of over a working life, and training that fits too snugly turns useless the moment the equipment moves on. What lasts is the ability to read a stiff manual, to reason over a drawing, to put a clean question to a colleague. Those abilities come by a long detour, and they look pointless at the very moment they are being taught, which is what makes them easy to cut. So we save on what prepares people best and pay later in failed career changes. I am not defending theory against the workbench. I say that the workbench with no detour turns out interchangeable hands.
